Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

inlavanilla 0.1.0

  • Initial version. inla_vanilla() approximates the posterior of any log-posterior written on an unconstrained scale with the INLAvaan pipeline: a Laplace approximation, a VB mean correction (by a deterministic degree-5 cubature rule), skew-normal marginals with the volume correction, and the log marginal likelihood. sampling() gives Gaussian-copula draws of the parameters or of any function of them. print(), summary() and plot() methods report the fit and its diagnostics.
  • loo() and waic() estimate predictive accuracy from the fit and a pointwise log-likelihood loglik(theta, ...), by the deterministic second-order Taylor approximation of Alhyari et al. (2026): no refits and no draws. The results work with loo::loo_compare(). A new vignette, “Model comparison with LOO and WAIC”, shows how. Both follow the fit’s silent, for the warnings of loglik too, and pass any other object on to the loo package’s functions of the same name.
  • The VB correction (vb) and the skew-normal marginals (marginals = "skewnormal" or "gaussian") can each be switched off, down to the Laplace approximation alone.
  • The VB correction uses a degree-5 rule built on a regular simplex, with at most (m + 1)(m + 2) + 1 nodes, against 2m^2 + 1 before, all within 3 posterior SDs. With a gradient it makes about half the calls at large m, with the same accuracy. Without one, it takes the expected gradient from values of logpost alone, by Stein’s identity on the same nodes, instead of finite-difference gradients: at most (m + 1)(m + 2) calls per sweep instead of (m + 1)(2m^2 + 1), so it costs about as much as finding the mode. For the 39-parameter SEM of the Rcpp article that is 8,200 calls instead of 487,000. This VB mean is exact when the log-posterior is a polynomial of degree four in whitened coordinates (six with a gradient). On test models it was a median 0.015 posterior SDs from exact VB, but up to about 0.1 on strongly skewed posteriors, where a gradient gives about 0.03.
  • Two website articles, “Speeding up with Rcpp” and “Gradients with RTMB”, fit a structural equation model with 39 parameters from a log-posterior written in R, in C++ with an analytic gradient, and in R for RTMB, which gives the gradient by automatic differentiation, and compare the routes for speed and accuracy.
  • A website article, “Multilevel models”, fits a linear mixed model with the random effects integrated out, and checks its marginals against brms.
  • A website article, “Diagnostic classification models”, fits the DINA model to the ECPE data with the latent classes summed out, checks its marginals against Stan, and classifies examinees from draws.
  • A website article, “Correlation matrices”, puts an LKJ prior on the correlation matrix of a multivariate normal, through its canonical partial correlations on the atanh scale, fits it to the Holzinger and Swineford tests, checks the marginals against Stan, and gives the reliability of each scale from draws.
  • A website article, “Binary factor analysis”, fits a one-factor model for binary items in the delta parameterisation, with the factor integrated out by Gauss-Hermite quadrature over the counts of the response patterns.
  • Three output levels: by default each stage prints one line; verbose = TRUE adds a full diagnostic of each stage (the optimiser’s report, how the Hessian was taken, the posterior correlations, the VB iterations, a line per marginal with the flagged values marked, and the calls each stage made); silent = TRUE prints nothing and muffles warnings, for simulations. The default output is what verbose = TRUE used to give, so code that passed verbose = FALSE to keep a fit quiet should now pass silent = TRUE. The warnings raised during a fit are kept in fit$warnings whatever the level.
  • While a stage runs, its line is the stage’s sentence with a counter, as in INLAvaan (“Fitting 4/6 skew-normal marginals”), not a bar as wide as the console. After two seconds it ends with the time so far, or the time left where the work is known in advance (the marginals and loo()), in the place where the finished line shows the time taken. The lines, loo()’s included, follow the cli.progress_show_after option when it is set (half a second otherwise), so a knitr or Quarto setup chunk can keep them out of a rendered document.
  • The diagnostics follow INLAvaan’s. Each parameter has the Newton step at the mode in posterior SDs (mode_shift_sigma), the VB shift on the scale of logpost (vb_shift) and in posterior SDs (vb_shift_sigma), with the Kullback-Leibler divergence of each shifted marginal (kld), and unscanned_mass, the mass each fitted skew-normal puts outside the scanned window; the VB columns are NA when vb = FALSE. The fit also records the condition number of the Hessian in posterior-SD units (hess_cond). summary() and verbose = TRUE show the unscanned mass.
  • A fit whose checks look off ends with one warning, of class inlavanilla_diagnostics_warning, headed “Fit diagnostics flagged N potential issues”, in INLAvaan’s words and at its levels: a Newton step at the mode above 0.1 posterior SDs (whatever nlminb()’s return code, with its message and a hint), an NMAD above 0.1, an unscanned mass above 0.05, a VB shift above 1 SD, and a Hessian condition number above 1e8; heavy tails are inlavanilla’s own check. Like INLAvaan, the fit only records the VB fallback. summary() flags the same checks at the same levels, and also a ridge bend above 0.25 nats, where the marginal SD may be about 10% too small, and a mean gap (between the skew-normal and VB means) above 0.1 SDs; its lines list every flagged parameter, worst first, with its value (names only for the heavy-tails check, which is yes or no). Healthy fits stay silent. A new vignette, “Diagnostics”, explains every check, with citations of Jamil and Rue (2026a).
  • summary() prints the fit first (the log marginal likelihood, and the calls and time each stage took), then the posterior marginals, then the diagnostics, each under its own heading. Its table of diagnostics (VB shift, NMAD, unscanned mass, ridge bend and mean gap) has numbers formatted as a tibble prints them and the flagged values in red. One line gives the largest value of each skew-normal check that passes, and each flagged check has a line of its own.
  • The tables of print() and summary() number their rows, as a tibble does, and line up the decimal points down each column. The posterior marginals still give each parameter to three significant figures of its posterior SD, and a value that rounds to zero no longer prints as “-0.000”.
  • print() and summary() open with the log marginal likelihood and whether the fit converged, with the iterations and the time the fit took. Converged means that the computation reached its solution: no further Newton step at the mode, and no further fixed-point step at the VB mean, would move a parameter by more than 0.1 posterior SDs. The second is a new check, vb_step_sigma in diagnostics(fit, type = "param"): where the fallback optimiser of the VB correction lands was not checked before. A correction that has not settled is flagged and raises a warning.
  • Printed output is never wider than 80 columns, or the console if it is narrower: the summaries, the verbose report and the fit-time warning wrap their long lines. The rendered documentation is 76 columns wide, so that no output scrolls sideways on the website.
  • diagnostics(fit) and diagnostics(fit, type = "param") return the checks as numbers, with the names, order and print formats of INLAvaan’s diagnostics(), followed by inlavanilla’s own. plot(fit, type = "sn_fit") and type = "sn_fit_log" draw each skew-normal fit against the scan it was fitted to, as INLAvaan’s plot does, from the scans the fit now keeps in fit$scan.
  • The check of a user grad also compares it with finite differences one curvature scale from init, so a gradient that is wrong by a constant factor is caught even when init is at the mode.
  • print() names the approximation on its header rule (“Skew-normal + VB”, “Skew-normal”, “Laplace + VB” or “Laplace”), as summary() now does, instead of the run time, which summary() still reports. It ends with a line when the fit raised warnings and one when summary() flags any check, so a fit run with silent = TRUE does not look clean when it is not.
  • summary() reports the 2.5%, 50% and 97.5% quantiles by default, as R-INLA does, instead of adding the quartiles, so its table fits in 80 columns and matches print(). Pass probs for others.
  • print() and summary() wrap long lines to the console width (the width option in R Markdown and Quarto), and split a table too wide for it into blocks of columns, as R does for a matrix.
  • The VB correction no longer stops with “NA/NaN gradient evaluation” when logpost is -Inf at some of its nodes, which reach up to 3 posterior SDs from the mode, as near a boundary of the support. Its fallback optimiser now moves away from those nodes. If it finds a VB mean where logpost is finite at every node, the fit goes ahead. Otherwise, as for a posterior truncated within reach of the nodes, the fit stops with an error that says so and suggests a reparameterisation or vb = FALSE.
  • With a gradient, a VB fallback that lands short of settled is rerun once from where it landed. That happens when the optimiser starts where a node fails, and it then reported convergence well short of the VB mean: 0.29 posterior SDs on a one-parameter posterior with a boundary. Fits whose fallback settles are unchanged, and verbose = TRUE reports the rerun.
  • A VB fixed-point step over 1.5 posterior SDs is now cut to 1.5, and the iteration goes on; only two such steps in a row hand over to the fallback optimiser. INLAvaan hands over at the first step over 1 SD, but on a skewed posterior the first step overshoots and the iteration then comes back. On a DINA model with 63 parameters and a gradient the handover cost 54,000 calls to reach the point that six fixed-point steps reach.
